# The .ezpkg file

This page is for administrators and developers who download, upload, unpack or build package archives. It answers:
what format an `.ezpkg` file is, what is inside, which checks it must pass on import, and how to look into one
without installing it.

## Contents

1. [The format](#the-format)
2. [What is inside](#what-is-inside)
3. [File names](#file-names)
4. [How Exponential reads an archive](#how-exponential-reads-an-archive)
5. [The checks before anything is written](#the-checks-before-anything-is-written)
6. [Opening an .ezpkg by hand](#opening-an-ezpkg-by-hand)
7. [How the 7x archives are built](#how-the-7x-archives-are-built)
8. [Related pages](#related-pages)

## The format

An `.ezpkg` file is a **gzip compressed tar archive** of one package directory. Nothing else: no header, no
signature, no manifest besides the package's own definition file. The suffix comes from `eZPackage::suffix()`
(`ezpkg`). When the kernel exports a package itself, `eZPackage::exportToArchive()` writes a tar archive and
compresses it with zlib; it can also write `tar.bz2` and `zip`, but `tar.gz` and `ezpkg` are the same thing and the
default.

The JSON format of a package is an `.ezpkg` too, with the same layout; only the definition file and the documents
differ. See [Classic and JSON packages](classic-and-json-packages.md).

## What is inside

The archive holds the **contents** of the package directory, not the directory: `package.xml` is at the top of the
archive, not inside a folder named after the package. A typical layout:

| Path in the archive | What it is | Written by |
|---|---|---|
| `package.xml` (or `package.json`) | The definition: name, type, version, dependencies, install items | `eZPackage::storePackageFile()` |
| `documents/` | Documents named in `<documents>`, for example `LICENCE` | `eZPackage::documentDirectory()` |
| `files/<collection>/<file type>/` | Files named in `<files>`: thumbnails, images, design files (`files/default/thumbnail/thumbnail.png`) | `eZPackage::appendFile()` |
| `simplefiles/` | Files kept by key, such as images of content objects (`simplefiles/24ec46f7.jpg`) | `eZPackage::appendSimpleFile()` |
| `settings/` | The install scripts of a site package | the package author |
| `ezcontentclass/` | One XML document per content class (`class-article.xml`) | the `ezcontentclass` handler |
| `ezcontentobject/` | `contentobjects.xml` and one `object-<remote id>.xml` per object | the `ezcontentobject` handler |
| `ezextension/` | `extension-<name>.xml` and the extension's files | the `ezextension` handler |
| `sql/[<database type>/]` | SQL files of `ezsql` items | the `ezdb` handler |

`exportToArchive()` copies `documents`, `files`, `simplefiles`, `settings` and the `sub-directory` of every install
item, so a file outside those directories does not survive an export. The `.cache/` directory that the local
repository keeps next to `package.xml` is never part of a package.

Listing two real archives from the package server:

```bash
curl -s https://exponential.packages.exponential.earth/exponential/6.0/6.0.15/sevenx_multisite.ezpkg | tar -tzf -
curl -s https://exponential.packages.exponential.earth/exponential/6.0/6.0.15/sevenx_classes.ezpkg | tar -tzf - | head
```

```text
documents/
documents/LICENCE
ezcontentclass/
ezcontentclass/class-real_video.xml
ezcontentclass/class-comment.xml
...
```

## File names

| Where | Name | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Package server | `<name>.ezpkg` | `sevenx_multisite.ezpkg` |
| Export from Setup > Packages or `ezpm export` (classic) | `<name>-<version>-<release>.ezpkg` | `mypackage-1.0.0-1.ezpkg` |
| Export in the JSON format | `<name>-<version>-<release>.json.ezpkg` | `mypackage-1.0.0-1.json.ezpkg` |

The name of the file does not matter on import: the package's name comes from `<name>` in its definition
(`eZPackage::importUnaudited()`), and the format from which definition file is at the top. The setup wizard's
upload strips a `-<digit>.<digits>-<digit>.ezpkg` ending from the file name when it reports what it imported
(`eZStepSiteTypes::uploadPackage()`).

## How Exponential reads an archive

`eZPackage::import()` (and `importUnaudited()` behind it) works in this order:

1. Scan the tar headers (`expPackageArchive::scan()`, next section), then open the archive through
   `compress.zlib://`, as a GNU tar archive when its first header carries the `ustar` magic, and as an old V7 tar
   archive when it does not (`eZPackage::archiveTarType()`): packages written by the 3.x releases are V7 archives.
2. Extract only `package.xml` and `package.json` (plain files only, never a link) into a temporary directory below
   the cache directory (`packages/import/`), read the definition, and delete the temporary copy.
3. Refuse the package when its name is not valid (`STATUS_INVALID_NAME`), or when a package of that name already
   exists in the repository (`STATUS_ALREADY_EXISTS`).
4. Choose the repository: the one passed in, else the directory made from `<vendor>`.
5. Check every entry of the archive (next section).
6. Extract the whole archive into `var/storage/packages/<repository>/<name>/` and read the package back. Every
   extracted file gets mode 0644 and every directory 0755 (within the installation's file mode limits), whatever
   modes the archive gives (`expPackageArchiveModes`).

The import of an archive is recorded in the audit trail as `system.package.import`, with the archive's SHA-256
and never its content (see `doc/eng-us/bc/6.0/audit.md`).

## The checks before anything is written

`eZPackageUploadInspector` holds the rules. `eZPackage::importUnaudited()` calls its `entriesProblem()` for every
archive it extracts, so the setup wizard, `ezpm import` and the upload page are all covered:

| Check | Refusal code | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Every tar header readable, its checksum right, no data cut off | `unreadable` | |
| Not a PAX archive (tar types `x` and `g`); pack with `tar --format=gnu` (GNU tar) or `tar --format=gnutar` (bsdtar, macOS) | `tar_pax` | |
| Only the tar types the reader handles: `0`, `5` and a GNU long name `L`; `\0` in a V7 archive; links and devices are refused below as `unsafe_type` | `tar_entry_type` | |
| A GNU long name at most 4096 bytes and not a multiple of 512 bytes | `tar_long_name` | |
| At most `MaxEntries` entries | `too_many_entries` | `50000` |
| Every path relative, without `..`, a back slash, NUL or a control character | `unsafe_path` | |
| Every entry a plain file or a directory (no links, no devices) | `unsafe_type` | |
| Unpacked size at most `MaxUnpackedSize` | `too_large_unpacked` | `2147483648` (2 GiB) |
| The vendor gives a usable repository directory name | (import refused) | |

The administration's upload page (`package/upload`) runs the full `inspect()` first, which adds:

| Check | Refusal code | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| The uploaded name ends in an allowed suffix | `suffix` | `AllowedSuffixes[]`: `ezpkg`, `tar.gz`, `tgz` |
| The file is at most `MaxArchiveSize` bytes | `too_large` | `268435456` (256 MiB) |
| The file starts with the gzip signature | `not_gzip` | |
| A definition file at the top, well formed, at most 16 MiB, with a valid name | `no_definition`, `definition_malformed`, ... | |

The tar header checks (the first four rows) run before the archive library reads a single entry, header by header,
with the data blocks skipped by their size: the library's GNU reader looped until `max_execution_time` on a header
type it does not know (a PAX archive, which Python's `tarfile` writes by default since 3.8 and `bsdtar` writes for
names that are not ASCII), and read a long name into memory in whatever size the header gave. A long name whose size
is a multiple of 512 bytes is refused because the reader then skips the real entry header; GNU tar stores the name
with a closing NUL, so a name of 511, 1023, ... or 4095 bytes cannot be imported (the message names the limit of
4096 bytes in that case as well). A package packed by GNU tar, by
bsdtar with `--format=gnutar` or `--format=ustar`, or by Exponential's export passes.

The limits are in `settings/package.ini [UploadSettings]`; change them in `settings/override/package.ini.append.php`.

```ini
[UploadSettings]
MaxArchiveSize=268435456
MaxUnpackedSize=2147483648
MaxEntries=50000
AllowedSuffixes[]
AllowedSuffixes[]=ezpkg
AllowedSuffixes[]=tar.gz
AllowedSuffixes[]=tgz
```

> **Note**
> `eZPackage::parseDOMTree()` also refuses a definition whose `<version><number>`, `<version><release>` or
> `<type value>` is not a plain token of up to 64 letters, digits and `._+-` (`eZPackage::isValidDefinitionToken()`).
> Such a package is not read at all. See [package.xml reference](package-xml-reference.md).

## Opening an .ezpkg by hand

You need nothing but `tar`. Work in a scratch directory of your own, never in `var/storage/packages/`.

```bash
# list the entries
tar -tzf sevenx_multisite.ezpkg

# print the definition without unpacking anything else
tar -xzOf sevenx_multisite.ezpkg package.xml

# unpack into a new directory
mkdir sevenx_multisite && tar -xzf sevenx_multisite.ezpkg -C sevenx_multisite

# check a package without importing it (from the installation root)
php ezpm.php validate sevenx_multisite.ezpkg
```

`ezpm validate` checks the definition, every document the install items name, and, for a JSON package, the schema
and the checksums; it prints `PASS` or `FAIL` and exits with 1 on failure (see
[the JSON package format](../../../bc/6.0/package-json-format.md)). To bring an archive into an installation, see
[Downloading a package by hand](../package-server/downloading-a-package-by-hand.md) and
[Import versus install](import-versus-install.md).

## How the 7x archives are built

The 7x packages are kept as plain folders in Git
([se7enxweb/sevenx-ezpackage](https://github.com/se7enxweb/sevenx-ezpackage), `packages/<name>/`).
`packages/build.sh` turns each folder into an archive from inside the folder, which is why there is no top folder:

```bash
cd "${folder%/}"
tar -zcf ../${folder}.ezpkg "${EXCLUDES[@]}" *
```

`EXCLUDES` leaves out version control files (`.git`, `.gitignore`, `.gitattributes`, `.gitmodules`, `.svn`,
`.hg`), editor and system leftovers (`.DS_Store`, `.idea`, `.vscode`, `*~`, `*.swp`) and `node_modules`. How a
built archive reaches the server is described in
[How a release reaches the package server](../package-server/how-a-release-reaches-the-package-server.md).
